title: First Aid Essentials
summary: Learn how to respond to emergencies: scene safety, CPR, bleeding, burns, choking, seizures, stroke and a home first aid kit. Course for awareness; take a practical course to be certified.
audience: Everyone: students, parents, teachers, workers and community volunteers

lessons.title: First aid principles and scene safety

body.p: First aid is the immediate help given to an injured or ill person before professional medical care arrives. Its aims are to preserve life, prevent the condition from getting worse, and promote recovery. First aid does not replace a doctor, and anyone seriously hurt should be taken to a health facility.

list: Danger: check the scene is safe for you, the casualty and bystanders. Do not become a second casualty.
Response: speak loudly and gently tap the shoulders. Is the person awake?
Send for help: call the local emergency number or ask someone to do it.
Airway: make sure the mouth and throat are clear and open.
Breathing: look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
Circulation: control severe bleeding and start CPR if needed.

body.p: Emergency numbers differ by country, so learn yours. Wear gloves if available and wash your hands after helping. Be calm, introduce yourself, ask permission to help, and keep the person warm and reassured.

body.tip: Never move a person with a suspected neck or back injury unless there is immediate danger such as fire.

body.p: If a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, they are in cardiac arrest. Send for help at once, ask for a defibrillator (AED) if one is available, and start cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

list: Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, with the other hand on top.
Push hard and fast, about 5 to 6 cm deep, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.
Allow the chest to rise fully between compressions.
If trained, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. A cycle of 30 compressions and 2 breaths is 32 actions.
If untrained, or unwilling to give breaths, do hands-only CPR with continuous compressions.
Do not stop until help takes over, an AED tells you to, or the person starts breathing normally.

body.p: At 100 to 120 compressions a minute, one compression takes between 0.5 and 0.6 seconds. Many people keep this rhythm by humming a song with a steady beat. Take turns if you can, as CPR is tiring. An AED gives spoken instructions; follow them.

body.tip: Children and babies need smaller, gentler compressions and different technique. Take a practical course with a qualified instructor to learn them.

body.p: Severe bleeding can kill within minutes. Apply firm, direct pressure on the wound with a clean pad or cloth, and keep pressing. Do not remove the pad if blood soaks through; add another on top. If a limb is bleeding heavily and pressure does not control it, a tourniquet may be used only by someone trained, as it carries serious risks.

list: Wash your hands, then rinse the wound with clean running water.
Clean around it with mild soap and cover with a sterile dressing.
Seek care for deep cuts, animal bites, wounds with dirt that cannot be removed, or if the person has not had a tetanus vaccine.
Cool the burn with cool running water for at least 20 minutes.
Remove rings or tight clothing near the area unless stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with clean cling film or a non-fluffy dry dressing.
Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or oils. Do not burst blisters.
Get medical help for large burns, burns on the face, hands or genitals, and burns in children.

body.p: Choking happens when something blocks the airway. If the person can cough, speak or breathe, encourage them to keep coughing. If they cannot breathe, cannot cough effectively or go quiet, act immediately.

list: Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If that fails, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind, make a fist above the navel, grasp it with the other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards.
Alternate between 5 back blows and 5 thrusts.
If the person becomes unresponsive, call for help and start CPR.

body.p: Babies need a different technique, using back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts. Learn this in a practical course.
Help the person sit upright and stay calm. Help them use their reliever inhaler as prescribed. If there is no improvement, or they struggle to speak, get emergency help immediately.

Fainting is a brief loss of consciousness, often from low blood flow to the brain. Lay the person down and raise their legs. Check breathing. Most people recover quickly, but seek advice if it was the first time or they were injured.

list: Stay calm and note the time the seizure started.
Clear space around the person and protect the head with something soft.
Do not hold them down and never put anything in their mouth.
When the jerking stops, turn them onto their side (recovery position) and stay with them.
Call for emergency help if it lasts more than 5 minutes, repeats, or the person is injured or pregnant.

body.p: Use FAST to spot a stroke: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Treatment works best when started early, so do not wait.

Signs of a heart attack include chest pain or pressure that may spread to the arm, jaw or back, sweating and breathlessness. Help the person sit down and rest and call emergency services. Shock from severe blood loss or injury shows as pale cold skin and a fast weak pulse; lay the person down and keep them warm.

lessons.title: Home first aid kit and common conditions

body.p: Every home, school and workplace should have a first aid kit that is checked every few months. Replace used and expired items.

list: Disposable gloves and a face shield for CPR.
Sterile dressings, bandages, adhesive plasters and tape.
Antiseptic wipes and saline for rinsing.
Scissors, tweezers and a thermometer.
Oral rehydration salts.
Foil blanket and a card with emergency numbers.

body.p: Diarrhoea can cause dangerous dehydration, especially in children. Give frequent small sips of oral rehydration solution made from the correct packaged salts mixed with the stated amount of clean water. Continue feeding and breastfeeding. Get medical help if there is blood in the stools, high fever, constant vomiting, or signs of dehydration such as very dry mouth, sunken eyes or very little urine.

For fever, keep the person comfortable, give fluids and follow the dosing guidance on the medicine label or from a pharmacist. In areas with malaria, fever needs testing. If someone swallows poison or an overdose of medicine, call your poison centre or emergency service and keep the container. Do not make the person vomit.

body.tip: Take a certified first aid course from a recognised organisation such as the Red Cross or Red Crescent. Practice with an instructor is the best way to learn.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check at the scene of an accident?
In DRSABC, what does the S stand for?
How deep should adult chest compressions be?
What rate of compressions is recommended?
What is the usual CPR ratio for a trained rescuer?
What should you do for severe bleeding?
How long should a burn be cooled with running water?
Which should NOT be put on a burn?
An adult is choking and cannot cough or breathe. What is the first action?
options: Push on the stomach of a baby

quiz.q: What should you do during a seizure?
options: Put a spoon in the mouth
Protect the head and do not restrain

quiz.q: What does the F in FAST stand for?
When should you call emergency help for a seizure?
options: Only if the person is a child
If it lasts more than 5 minutes

quiz.q: What is the best way to treat dehydration from diarrhoea?
options: Oral rehydration solution in small frequent sips

quiz.q: What should you do if someone swallows poison?
options: Call poison centre or emergency service and keep the container
